analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for households to erase debts in bankruptcy and pushes many into multi-year repayment plans instead.
analysis.headline: Introduced by the Senate Majority Leader with no cosponsors, the bill went straight onto the Senate calendar and never received a vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal bankruptcy law using a formula-based income test: if a household's income clears a threshold, the law would presume the filing is "abuse" and push the debtor out of Chapter 7 (wiping debts clean) and into Chapter 13 (repaying creditors for years). Everyone filing would first have to complete credit counseling and a financial-management course to get a discharge, gaps between bankruptcies would lengthen, and several debtor protections — including the automatic stay against evictions — would be trimmed. Scattered through the bill are provisions that help particular groups, most notably putting child support and alimony at the front of the repayment line and requiring credit card companies to print minimum-payment warnings on statements.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card banks and other unsecured lenders would gain the most: a formula-based "means test" would presume abuse and push higher-income debtors out of Chapter 7 liquidation into Chapter 13 repayment plans, gaps between discharges would stretch from six years to eight (Chapter 7) and six to five (Chapter 13), liens would ride along longer in Chapter 13 plans, and more documentation burdens would raise the cost of filing. A minority of debtors would also gain: child support and alimony claims would jump to first priority, domestic support obligations would become nearly impossible to discharge, and credit card statements would carry minimum-payment warnings.

how_it_helps.text: A formula-based means test would presume "abuse" if a debtor's income, minus IRS-standard expenses, exceeds the lesser of $15,000 or 25 percent of nonpriority unsecured debts over five years, converting many Chapter 7 wipeouts into Chapter 13 repayment plans for creditors.
Every individual debtor would have to complete a briefing from an approved nonprofit credit counseling agency before filing and a personal financial management course before discharge.
The waiting period between Chapter 7 discharges would stretch from six years to eight, and between Chapter 13 discharges to five.

Child support and alimony would move to first priority among creditor claims, become nondischargeable, and remain collectible through license suspension, tax-refund interception, and credit reporting even during a bankruptcy case.

Credit card statements would have to carry a warning that making only the minimum payment increases interest and repayment time, plus a toll-free number giving an estimate of months to pay off the balance; retroactive finance charges on paid-off balances would be banned.

analysis.who_pays: Households seeking bankruptcy relief would pay: a new income test would force many into multi-year repayment plans instead of a fresh start, mandatory credit counseling and financial-management courses would add cost and delay, secured lenders would keep their liens longer, eviction protections would narrow, and debtors' attorneys would face fee reimbursements and penalties if a judge calls a filing frivolous.

drawbacks.text: The credit counseling requirement would force every filer — including families in genuine crisis — through an extra paid gatekeeper before they can reach the courthouse, and the bill itself concedes some districts may not have enough approved agencies to handle the demand.

Rebutting the presumption of abuse requires itemized documentation of "special circumstances" under penalty of perjury, a burden that would push borderline households into five-year repayment plans or out of bankruptcy entirely.

Debtors' attorneys could be ordered to reimburse trustee legal fees and pay civil penalties for filings a court finds frivolous, which would raise legal costs and scare lawyers away from marginal clients.

Exceptions to the automatic stay would let landlords evict nonpaying tenants more quickly, and the homestead exemption would be capped and subject to a two-year residency rule, weakening shelter protections for some filers.

The bill is a grab-bag: bankruptcy titles sit alongside an unrelated methamphetamine statute, a voiding of a Hydro-Quebec power contract, and new sentencing minimums, making it hard for any legislator to vote on the core issue alone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine gains — first-priority child support, mandatory minimum-payment warnings, and standardized reaffirmation disclosures — are real but modest, and the same bill hands secured and unsecured lenders their long-sought means test, longer discharge gaps, and new attorney liability. For the households the bankruptcy system exists to serve, the cost side dominates: more paperwork, a mandatory counseling fee, a harder path to a fresh start, and faster evictions. The bill's own sense-of-Congress language admits that indiscriminate credit extension drives consumer insolvency, yet its remedies fall almost entirely on the debtor rather than the lender.

outcome.mechanism: The Majority Leader put his own bill straight onto the Senate calendar without a committee stop, and it sat there while the clock ran out on the 106th Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Trent Lott, the Senate Majority Leader, introduced the bill on September 14, 2000.
The next day it was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 807, skipping any committee consideration.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with the bill still on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households facing bankruptcy came out ahead: the more forgiving pre-reform law stayed in place, so Chapter 7 remained open without a means test or mandatory counseling. Lenders gained nothing and had to wait for a later Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumer debtors who kept the old law

for.name: Trent Lott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it read twice and placed directly on the Senate calendar with no committee referral or hearing.

for.name: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for years for a means-tested bankruptcy law that would push more debtors into full repayment plans; this bill was the product of that campaign.

against.name: Consumer groups and bankruptcy judges and attorneys
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed means-test bankruptcy bills as obstacles placed between struggling households and debt relief.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill carried a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors, so any partisan split never showed itself in the record.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: The means test, longer discharge gaps, and tighter reaffirmation and lien rules would let these lenders collect more from households that today walk away from debts. Every dollar recovered is a dollar the debtor keeps paying.

Every bankruptcy filer would have to buy a counseling briefing before filing and a financial-management course before discharge, guaranteeing the agencies customers. The bill tries to police them — nonprofit boards, no commissions, fee caps, and a ban on reporting counseling status to credit bureaus — but the mandate itself is the industry's gain.

industries.industry: Secured lenders (auto finance, mortgage, consumer credit)
industries.note: Chapter 13 plans would keep liens intact until all debts are paid, rules on valuing and stripping down car and personal-property liens would tighten, and debtors would have to act within 45 days or lose possession of collateral.

industries.industry: Wall Street derivatives and securitization counterparties
industries.note: Swap and netting agreements would be exempted from the automatic stay and protected from trustee avoidance, and failed banks' qualified financial contracts would move faster through FDIC receivership — insulating derivatives counterparties from the freezes that ordinary debtors face.

Attorneys would have to certify they investigated each petition and could be ordered to reimburse trustees and pay civil penalties if a filing is found frivolous — a liability risk that would make lawyers more expensive or harder to hire for exactly the people bankruptcy exists to help.
